translations.text: The life and conduct of the holy and honored ascetic fathers, Apa Longinus and Apa Lucius, his spiritual father. They completed their honored lives on the second day of the month of Meshir, in the peace of God. Amen.

Those who have completed lives of conduct fitting for people who wear flesh—where are the tongues of flesh to speak their praises? Those who have surpassed the human measure in their conduct, whose achievements have exceeded the burden borne by those who wear flesh, as though they had almost no flesh upon them—what tongue of flesh can speak of their honor? People of this kind need the tongues of bodiless beings to speak their praises, just as they have completed their angelic lives. The burden of the flesh did not prevent them in any way from becoming equal to angels and fulfilling the way of life of those in heaven while living on earth, according to what the holy apostle said: “But our citizenship is in heaven, from where we await our Savior, our Lord, who will transform our lowliness into the likeness of the body of his glory.”

For this reason, when I wished to set down the account of the holy Apa Longinus and his spiritual father, Apa Lucius, who completed their lives—or, rather, their contests and struggles—I was perplexed within myself, knowing my own weakness and the loftiness of that holy man's virtues. I was like someone standing beneath a very high rock, attempting to scale that rock or climb up it, perplexed on every side about how I could manage to climb onto that rock. Allow me to say, “The rock was Christ.” For wherever the saints are, the Lord of the saints is there. For he who did not disdain to go up the mountain with Peter and John also did not disdain to dwell with Apa Longinus and Apa Lucius, his father, in the place where they were. And perhaps, just as that vision showed Peter and John who it was who had gone up onto that rock, so he also instructed Apa Lucius and Apa Longinus in the upright faith, which many attained through them, as we will make clear as we proceed.

Nevertheless, knowing my own weaknesses, I wished to remain silent about the account of those saints because of their loftiness and my own insignificance. Yet I also saw judgment before my eyes, threatening me in this way: “Does cowardice of this kind please God? If you truly acknowledge that they are holy and worthy of praise, and that their conduct was so completely exalted, as you say, and that their life can build up those who will hear it, why do you choose silence instead of telling us the life of those saints? Even if you cannot tell us about the conduct of those saints, which is full of every virtue, nevertheless tell with humility whatever you can grasp, so that you do not seem to begrudge the benefit to the souls of those who will hear the life of those holy and praiseworthy men and follow them in some small part of it.”

Especially since the herald of truth, the teacher Paul, commands: “Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Look at the excellence of their way of life and imitate their faith.” And since God knows that the lives of those who lived according to his will would benefit those who hear about them, he recorded for us through his Holy Spirit the lives of the patriarchs and the rest of the saints who lived under the Old and New Covenants. This was so that we would not merely hear about them, but would imitate their way of life and ourselves inherit the promises God made to those who love him. So, reflecting on these things in my heart, I considered it necessary to begin the history of the saints and remind you of their conduct, knowing with certainty that “the remembrance of the righteous is a good remembrance,” and that “a good report gladdens the heart.” Especially since peoples rejoice when speaking of the righteous, according to what the wise Solomon said.

The conduct and life of our holy father Apa Longinus, who was from the monastic settlement of the Enaton at Alexandria.

He was a man of this kind. By his earthly ancestry, he came from a city in Lycia, but he was a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem, with his citizenship in heaven, according to the words of the wise Paul. While he was still a small boy, he came to love the philosophy of the monastic life. He went to a monastery in his own region of Lycia, called the monastery of Apa Hieronicus. When he was judged worthy to receive the holy monastic habit in that monastery, he was entrusted to a great ascetic named Apa Lucius, who was adorned with the words of the holy Scriptures and with discernment, the mother of all virtues. He also instructed him in the faith and in all the observances appropriate to the monastic life.

After he had spent some time living in the monastery in the virtues of Christ—that is, humility, vigilance, renunciation, and the other virtues of this kind—the superior of that monastery died. He was a quiet and peaceable man, and another was appointed in his place. Then a disturbance arose in the monastery’s church for this reason: everyone knew Apa Lucius, and they all looked to him as the one who would lead them after the man who had fallen asleep. When the holy man realized that a disturbance was about to arise on his account, he chose to leave them to themselves—that is, to leave that monastery so that the place could be at peace. Above all, he never stopped pursuing humility, in imitation of his Lord.

As he considered these things, he called his disciple Apa Longinus and said to him, “My son, we know that it is a serious matter to leave our monastery during our lifetime. But so that we do not become responsible for a disturbance of this kind and bring judgment upon ourselves, I think it is better for us to withdraw to a place by ourselves, according to what is written in Proverbs: ‘It is better to live in a corner on a roof than to live in a new house and in plastered places amid strife.’ It is therefore to our advantage to withdraw to a place by ourselves and devote ourselves to the salvation of our souls, for which we renounced the world and everything in it, rather than remain here and witness the ruin of our monastery.” This was the reason they left their monastery. Rather, it was an arrangement of God that came about so that he might reveal the gifts of his goodness, which cares for our bodies and souls through his chosen ones, and so that many might be saved through them.

When they left their monastery, they reached a quiet village in that same region of Lycia. They settled in a church in that village named after the honored holy martyr Theoctistus. This, too, did not happen merely by chance, but so that the wonders of God might be revealed, as was made clear by the meaning of the honored name of the martyr Theoctistus, which foretold what would happen in his place of prayer through these holy men. For Theoctistus is translated as “the one built by God.” As those holy men were built up in the martyr’s name through their ascetic practices and their many struggles, they in turn built up many souls through the wonders and healings that God performed through them in that place. After they settled there, many people came from the surrounding region, bringing the sick, especially those afflicted by unclean spirits, and laying them in that cemetery. They received healing through the prayers of that holy man.

For there was a woman possessed by an extremely violent unclean spirit. Through the demon within her, she caused great disturbances and commotion, so that she would tear the clothes and even the bodies of anyone who approached her. When they brought her before the servants of God and begged them to pray over her so that she might obtain healing through their intercession, she again began to convulse and attack those around her. Then she fell at their feet and remained there, being thrown about by the evil spirit that was with her, and foaming at the mouth. After crying out in a loud voice, she became like a dead person. Then the blessed Lucius, moved with compassion for her, began to pray and lay his hands on her. He instructed his disciple Longinus to pray as well, to lay his hands on her, and to make the sign of the cross over her. When they did this, the demon immediately came out of her, and she rose like someone waking from sleep, freed from the affliction that had been with her. From that day until her death, she served the sick in the martyrs’ shrine. This, then, was the first sign that God performed through them after they left the monastery and settled in that church.

I will also tell of another miracle that God performed through his servants. There was a man in that region who had a son of noble birth who had reached the age of boyhood. A woman named Flavia entrusted a document to the boy’s parents. They gave it to their son to keep safe. But the boy suddenly died, and his parents did not know where the document was. That woman, Flaviana, came looking for what she had entrusted to them, namely the document. They were at a loss and could not find it, because they did not know where the boy had put it. In great anger she threatened to make them her slaves—when these blessed men heard this, [?]—if they did not return her document to her. Then, as the boy’s parents continued to be harassed by that woman, they left their son without burying him and hurried to the place where the saints were. Large crowds followed them, consisting of their relatives and neighbors. They fell at the feet of Apa Lucius and Apa Longinus and pleaded with them, saying, “Pray to the Lord Christ, whose servants you are, that he may make the soul of our son who has died appear, so that through him we may learn where he put the document. A rich woman entrusted it to us, and she is now threatening to make us her slaves if we do not find the document and give it to her.”

When the blessed men heard these things from the boy’s parents, they felt compassion for them through the love and mercy of Christ that were within them. They quickly got up and followed them without any agitation or self-importance. When they reached the house where the dead boy was, they went into the place where the dead boy lay, bent their knees, and prayed. Since God wished to reveal the miracle to blessed Apa Longinus, who was full of virtue, he was immediately filled with the Holy Spirit. He took the boy’s hand in front of the crowd and said, “The God who raised Lazarus in those days is the same one who will now return your spirit to you, so that you may tell us where you put the rich woman’s document, so that she does not take your parents as slaves.” Immediately the boy’s spirit returned to him. He rose, sat up, and opened his mouth. With everyone standing there listening, he told them where the document was in the house. His parents also asked him about other matters of which they had no knowledge, and he answered them about everything they asked him. Then he immediately fell asleep. When the people of Lycia saw this miraculous deed that had taken place through the saints, they gave glory to God, who alone performs these miracles.

When news about them spread through that country, all the people brought to them their sick, suffering from every kind of illness, so that they might pray over them and heal them. They also bestowed great honors on them. When they grew weary of the enormous crowds that troubled them and of the glory people gave them—which they did not value because of their great humility—they decided to flee secretly and leave those districts. But when the people living around them learned of this, they kept watch over them, because they did not want to be deprived of their blessing and their presence among them. For they were the pride of that whole country because of the many miracles that took place through them.

Then the blessed Lucius took his disciple aside and said to him, “We cannot remain like this, bearing the empty praise of people, nor is it beneficial to our souls. So, my son, listen to me: get up secretly and go to Alexandria. I have heard about a monastery west of that city, called the Enaton, where there is great quiet in keeping with God’s will. Look for a man from Corinth named Gaius, who is the abbot of his own community, which he built in that place, and stay there with him. I hope in the Lord God our Savior that, wherever you are, he will not deprive me of living with you in the body. Even if some time passes while I am away from you, I trust in the Lord that I will certainly come to you, so that we may finish our course together in the place that the Lord will appoint for us according to his will. Wherever you may be, my son, flee from the empty praise of people. Go first to the shrine of Saint Menas and pray; then go to the Enaton and live in the monastery of Apa Gaius.”

When he had said these things, they prayed and greeted one another, and in this way he departed from him. When the blessed Apa Longinus arrived in Alexandria, he asked about the monastery of Apa Gaius in the Enaton, and some devout people showed him the way to it. When he came to the monastery, he knocked gently at the door. When the porter opened the door, he asked him, “Where are you from, and why have you come here?” Apa Longinus, who was truly humble, answered, “I am from the region of Lycia, and I have come here to become a monk.” For, because of his great humility, he could not bring himself to call himself a monk. He was wearing neither a hood nor a mantle, nor was it the custom of foreign monks to wear these garments in this way, but only a sleeveless tunic, a cloak, and a belt. These were what he himself was wearing when he came to the monastery. His hair had grown a little because of the many days he had spent on the journey by which he had come. For this reason they did not immediately recognize that he was a monk. The porter said to him, “You will not be able to become a monk here. For our prescribed psalm singing is extensive, and our eating, our sleeping, and the rest of our activities involve great hardship and toil, with no comfort in them. So take some loaves as a blessing. The Lord be with you.”

But the noble Apa Longinus did not argue or say a word to him. Instead, when he heard mention of the blessing, he accepted the loaves with the blessing and patiently remained outside the door for many days. In this too he imitated the great Anthony, who went to the great Paul the hermit, but, after the great hardship he had endured on the journey through the deserts, that great man did not receive him immediately. The blessed Anthony himself patiently remained at the doorway, saying, “I sought and I found, and I believe that the door will be opened to me.” Likewise, since this same Spirit dwelt in him, and he was pondering these things in his heart, he too patiently remained at the doorway until, through his great perseverance, he attained what he had in mind. As the porter continued to come out every day to do the tasks assigned to him, he would find him sitting at the doorway with great perseverance. He brought word to the abbot of the monastery, saying, “There is a young foreign man at the monastery doorway who has been there for several days, saying, ‘I want to become a monk.’ I have turned him away many times, but he has persevered until now.” The superior answered, “Since you have seen his perseverance, bring him inside the gate to stay with you. Let him remain and help you with your tasks, in whatever work you assign to him.”

Then the steward brought him to the gate, according to the instruction of the father of the monastery. He not only did everything the gatekeeper instructed him to do, but whenever any of the brothers gave him an instruction, he carried it out with great diligence and complete obedience. He continued in this way, doing such tasks for two years or more, and never told the brothers that he was a monk. But God, who always honors those who honor him, reveals what is hidden, and exalts the humble—who said with his truthful mouth, “They do not light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but put it on the lampstand so that it gives light to everyone in the house”—did not wish his chosen one to remain hidden. Instead, he revealed him as one who truly gives light and placed him on the spiritual lampstand, so that he would give light not only to those around him but also to others far away from him. He illuminated them through the abundance of his fruits and his virtuous deeds, as the account will reveal to us as the narrative proceeds.

There was a merchant from Lycia, the region of Apa Longinus, who knew him well while he was in his monastery. He happened to come to Alexandria on business. After going to the shrine of Saint Menas to pray, he also wished to visit the monastery of the blessed Gaius the priest, as was his custom, because he had great faith in that place. When he came to him to receive his blessing, he asked him to pray for him. While he was sitting at the church doorway, Saint Gaius spoke many words of instruction to him from the holy Scriptures for the salvation of his soul. The merchant looked and saw Apa Longinus, who had raised the dead man and had also performed many miracles in the region of Lycia. But he hesitated, thinking that it was not him, but someone who resembled him. For his hair had grown long over time, and he was suffering great hardship. For this reason, he did not recognize him with certainty. But there had been a mark on his face since his childhood. When the merchant looked carefully at the mark on his face, he said to Saint Gaius, “You have a great man here in this monastery who has performed many miracles.”

The superior said to him, “Which of the brothers are you saying this about?” The merchant said to him, “I am speaking about the man sweeping by the gate. This is Apa Longinus, who became famous in the region of Lycia, together with his spiritual father, Apa Lucius. He raised the dead and cast many demons out of people, and God worked many other healings through him in that region. When his fame spread throughout that region and everyone honored him, he left his spiritual father behind and fled, coming here secretly to escape the empty praise of people.” While he was saying these things about Saint Apa Longinus, Longinus was sweeping at the gate. Then the abbot called him and said to him, “Why did you conceal yourself from us and not tell us that you are a monk?” Immediately Apa Longinus, who was truly humble in his heart, fell at the feet of Gaius the priest and bowed before him, saying, “Forgive me, my father.” At once the superior ordered that the hair on his head, which had grown long, be shaved off. He prayed over him and put the headcloth and mantle on him according to the monastic dress of Alexandria. When the brothers in the monastery heard all these things about Apa Longinus, they regarded him as a great man who had attained perfection, and they began to honor him even more. But when Saint Apa Longinus saw that people were honoring him, he was distressed. All the more, he [?] remembered the instruction his spiritual father had given him: “Flee from the empty praise of people.”

Then he reflected within himself, saying, “I left my homeland because of the praise of people, and I parted from my father. How can I stay here when such a large crowd is honoring me?” For this reason he left that monastery. Some people who loved God had built him a small cell nearby, beside the monastery [?], by the sea. He lived in seclusion there, making cords. He toiled at his manual work so that he could find the means to give to those in need through the work of his hands. In this he imitated the holy apostle Paul, who says, “These hands served my needs and those of the people with me,” and, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” Many of the leading shipowners used to come to him and take the cords he made with his holy hands. They made them into crosses in the middle of their sails as a blessing, believing that his prayers would be a protection for them and that the Lord would keep their ships safe wherever they went. After a few days, three monks came to him and became his disciples.

One night, while he was sitting with his disciples, meditating on the word of God and doing manual work, he dozed off as he sat on his stool in the place where he worked. He was remembering the sacred psalmist David: “I will not give sleep to my eyes, slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, [?] a place for the Lord, a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.” As he sat that night, sleep overcame him, and he fell into a trance. It was as though a man stood before him and said to him, “Get up quickly and go to the seashore. There you will find your father, Apa Lucius. He has come to you from the countryside.” He got up immediately, without telling any of his disciples, and went to the seashore, to the place he had been told about in the revelation. He found the holy Apa Lucius, who had just come ashore from the boat. When they had greeted one another, the old man said to him, “Did I not tell you, my son, that I trust in Christ that wherever you go, I will come to you?” Then they glorified God because he had made them worthy to see one another, and because what was written had been fulfilled: “The deer gathered there and saw one another’s faces. They came out in their full number; not one of them was missing, because the Lord had commanded them, and his Spirit had gathered them together.” For the great trumpet of the prophets rightly called people like these deer, because deer love the wilderness and hunt the race of snakes as enemies. In the same way, these holy men flee the turmoil of the cities and live in deserted places. They also continually hunt the race of spiritual snakes, which are the spirits of wickedness.

The two of them walked along and went inside together. His disciples were sitting, meditating and working. When they saw the holy Apa Longinus walking with his father, they were amazed. They rose with great joy and greeted one another. After they had prayed, they sat down. Apa Longinus said to them, “This is your father from this day forward.” Then he told them what had been done to them in the vision concerning him. The holy Apa Lucius had Apa Longinus teach him too how to work on the [?]. From then on they continued serving God with great devotion, living together in great peace, each keeping his own assigned place in every service. Thus the fame of their conduct and their disciplined life filled the great city of Alexandria and all Egypt.

A woman had a disease in her breast that doctors call cancer. She had heard about the great Apa Longinus, that the Lord performed healings through him, so she set out in faith and went to find him. When she reached the seashore, she encountered the holy Apa Longinus splitting wood beside the seashore, as was his custom. She asked him, “Where is the servant of God, Apa Longinus?” He said, “What do you want with him?” She told him about the disease she had. He said to her, “What do you want with that man? He is nothing.” Then he made the sign of the cross over the diseased part of her body, saying, “May my Lord Jesus Christ act for you according to your faith.” The woman believed and turned back toward her home. When she had gone a short distance away from him, she was freed from the disease. When she entered the city, she told everyone about the healing she had received through the holy man. They asked her, “What does that man look like?” She described the features of his blessed face, and they told her that it was Apa Longinus who had healed her. The woman glorified God.

Oh, who can speak of the healings and miracles that God performed through him? If I wanted to speak of each of his healings individually, time would run out while I was still speaking. But I will tell a few of them and bring the account to an end here. I am holding back so that some people will not disbelieve because of the great number of miracles. For many people came to him from the city of Alexandria and its surrounding districts, wanting to find out where he was staying. They brought him everyone who was sick with any kind of illness, and he healed them all.

One day a woman brought him her son, who had a demon. His face had been twisted backward by the demon’s power, and it struck him every day, tormenting him. His mother begged the holy man to pray over him. He stretched out his hands and prayed, saying, “Lord Jesus Christ, you who work for our salvation, if it is your will, grant healing to this little boy.” As he did this, he breathed into the little boy’s face. Immediately the demon came out of him, and his face became as it had been before. They hurried home, giving glory to God.

When they saw that many people were coming to them, it became necessary for them to bake some loaves for their own needs, for strangers, and for those who came to them. Then, while the loaves were spread out in the sun, a heavy rain suddenly poured down. Immediately the holy Apa Longinus stood up and prayed, saying, “God of all and maker of creation, command this rain to pass us by.” Immediately the clouds moved away from the place where the loaves were, and not a single drop fell on the loaves. His prayer had become like a shelter over the place where the loaves were, and not a single drop fell on the loaves.

Once again, while he was sitting in his cell, making cords and meditating on the word of God, a woman came to him with a disease in her hand that doctors call “amianton,” meaning incurable. She came around behind the cell and pleaded with him, saying, “Please be kind and pray for me.” But he sternly told her to go away. She remained silent, afraid to speak. When he perceived through the Spirit the great suffering she was enduring, he got up and closed the opening of the window through which she was looking in. He said to her, “Go in peace. The Lord grants you healing.” The woman was healed from that very moment.

One day a man came to receive something from him and begged him to give him one of his hoods, so that it might serve as a protection for him. When he had received it, he left him. When he went home, there was a man there who was possessed by a demon. When he saw the man holding Apa Longinus’s hood, the demon threw him to the ground and cried out, saying, “Why have you brought Apa Longinus here to persecute people?” Those in the house were astonished at what the demon was saying. The man too was astonished and realized that these things had happened because of Apa Longinus’s hood. Immediately he took it and laid it on the demon-possessed man, saying, “In the name of the God [?] of my father Apa Longinus, come out of him!” Immediately the demon came out of him. When the people saw what had happened, they glorified God, who performs these wonders through his saints.

Another day, while he was sitting, the elders from the monastic settlement were sitting beside him, having come to visit him. While they were discussing the state of their souls [?], he immediately got up as though someone had called him. He left the cell and went to the harbor. He found a boat that had come from the south, with a holy elder aboard it. When the elder saw him, he greeted him with a holy kiss. The elder lifted his eyes to heaven and said, “Lord, did I not beg you not to let this holy man know that I was coming to him, so that he would not trouble himself to come out to meet me?” He turned to Apa Longinus and said to him, “My time to depart from this life has drawn near. For this reason the Lord sent me to you, so that you might place your hands over my eyes.” So the two of them walked together and entered Apa Longinus’s cell. After three days, the elder passed away in a good old age. The holy Apa Longinus placed his hand over his eyes, and he completed his life in a good old age.

Once again, he was going into the cell of one of his disciples, whose name was Arcadius. Arcadius was working on a [?] and was close to finishing it. Abba Longinus said to him, “My son Arcadius, hurry and finish it, because God will send for you now.” When he had finished the [?], he took him by the hand, laid him on the mat, and turned his face toward the east. Immediately the disciple peacefully gave his spirit into God’s hands.

On another day, they brought him a man possessed by a demon and begged him to drive it out of him. But Abba Longinus said to him with humility of heart, “I do not know what [?] for him. Instead, go to Abba Zeno, and I trust in God that he will grant him healing.” When they went to Abba Zeno, they begged him to pray over the man. When Abba Zeno began to pray, the demon cried out, “Do you think I am coming out because of you? Look, Abba Longinus is over there praying, and I am coming out because I am afraid of his prayers. Otherwise, I would not answer you.” When the unclean spirit had said this, it came out of the man.

He also had a disciple who had done things that were not right. When Abba Theodore of the Enaton learned about this, he came to him with some other elders, and they begged him to send the disciple away. But he would not listen to them, because perhaps the disciple would repent and God would forgive him—God, who does not desire the sinner’s death, but rather that he should repent and live. He only said this one thing to them: “Woe to us! We renounce the world and enter this monastic life, saying that we will become like the angels, yet instead we become worse than the unclean spirits.”

Another day an important shipowner came to him, bringing him a very large sum of money to give him. But he accepted nothing from him, saying, “We have no need of anything like this. Our manual work is enough for us. But please mount your donkey and go quickly to the landing place of Saint Peter. You will find a man there wearing clothes of a certain kind and with other distinguishing marks on his face—God has just revealed these things to me. Ask him, ‘Where are you going, and what is this you have with you?’”

The shipowner went quickly, as the elder had instructed. When he reached the landing place, he found the man about whom Apa Longinus had spoken to him. He approached him and spoke to him. But the man would not answer him at all because of the distress he was in. Instead, he was hurrying to leave the city and do what he had in mind. When the shipowner saw his anguish and how troubled he was, he said to him, “I have just come from the Enaton, from my father Apa Longinus. He is the one who sent me to you.” When the man heard the name of Apa Longinus, he stopped. The shipowner gave him the money, and the man told him about his distress, saying, “I owe many debts, and the creditors are putting pressure on me over them [?]. I decided to leave the city and hang myself because of the many troubles weighing on me. So that you may know the truth, here is the rope I have with me, with which I am going to hang myself.” He showed him the rope he was carrying.

The shipowner marveled at Apa Longinus’s words. He gave the gold to the man, and the man went home. The shipowner returned to Apa Longinus and told him everything that had happened. The elder said to him, “Believe me, my son: if we had neglected this even a little longer, God would have judged both of us for that man’s soul.”

At that time, when Emperor Marcian wanted to send an imperial official to Alexandria with the Tome of the impious Leo, he ordered the city of Alexandria to sign it, especially the monks of the Enaton. God revealed this matter to the holy Abba Longinus three months beforehand. In the revelation shown to him, he commanded him to gather all the monks of the Enaton and tell them what had happened. He also commanded them not to accept that doctrine at all or to sign it.

Abba Longinus gathered everyone in the monastic community and told them what the Lord had revealed to him in the vision. He instructed them to hold firmly to the Lord’s commandments and to struggle for the orthodox faith even to death. When they heard these things from Abba Longinus, they rejoiced greatly and consulted with one another, saying, “No one can put an end to this polluted doctrine except the one to whom the Lord revealed this mystery, informing him of the affliction destined to come.” Then they begged the blessed Abba Longinus to become their father and guide, and the superior over the monasteries of the Enaton.

After three months, the imperial agent arrived with that godless decree. The emperor had written to Acacius, the Augustal prefect who governed at that time, ordering him to compel the monks in the monastery to sign the defiled Tome of Leo. When the duke read the emperor’s letters, he copied them onto a diptych and sent them to the monks of the Enaton. It was written as follows: “Acacius, the Augustal prefect, writes to the holy, God-loving fathers, the monks of the monastery of the Enaton: Greetings. Since our lord the emperor, the sovereign ruler, has honored us with his sacred letters, ordering everyone to sign the Tome of Leo, bishop of Rome—and especially Your Holinesses, the monks of the Enaton—now, when you receive the letters from the imperial agent, you shall carry out the command of our lord the emperor, so that you may obtain gifts and honors from the great benefactor and warrior emperor on account of our wisdom.”

When the holy Apa Longinus received the letters, he gathered all the brothers together and read the diptych to them. When they heard it, they cried out together, anathematizing that filthy decree, its contents, the impious Leo, and everyone in communion with him. Then they wrote a letter to the Augustal prefect in these terms: “You are subject to the filthy decree of the emperor, but we, for our part, submit to the Almighty, who benefits all things through his providence. Let it therefore be made clear to your authority that none of us, from the least to the greatest, will tolerate accepting or even listening at all to that defiled and unlawful decree of the impious Leo. Rather, we are all ready to struggle to the death for the established teachings and the tradition of the sound faith of our holy and orthodox fathers, which they handed down to us. Let us not write many words to you, for it is better for us and beneficial to our souls to obey the decree of the Almighty rather than that of your emperor.”

When the duke received the letter, he understood its significance. He and the emperor’s magistrians became furious at the defenses presented by the holy men of the Enaton. They consulted together about having the magistrian take the army of soldiers and kill the monks of the Enaton. But the Lord, who frustrates the plans of rulers, revealed this to the holy elders Apa Lucius and Apa Longinus. They gathered all the brothers together, and Apa Longinus said to them, “I beg you, brothers, do not let any one of you be disturbed. Instead, listen to me: let each of you take some palm branches, and let us all go together to deceive the governor before he comes to us.” This proposal pleased the brothers. They took palm branches and went to the place called Lithazomenon, outside the city. The whole company of monks stood there. No one dared to enter the city, because this was their father’s command.

Then the magistrian came to wage war against the monks. When they reached them, he ordered the army to shoot arrows at the company of monks. The soldiers shot arrows at them. What a great wonder! The soldiers stood shooting [?] at the company of monks, yet none of them was harmed. They all sang this hymn with one voice, saying, “We have put our trust in the Lord. How can you say to our soul, ‘Fly away to the mountains like a bird’? For look, the sinners have drawn their bows and prepared their arrows on the bowstring, to shoot secretly at those who are upright in heart.” And also, “The sinners have drawn their swords and bent their bows to bring down the poor and needy, to slaughter those who are upright in heart.” Indeed, their swords entered their own hearts, and their arrows broke.

But the mighty soldier Apa Longinus, who fought for the truth to the point of death and showed by his own conduct that he dwelt under the shadow of the Most High, was not afraid of the arrows flying through the air. Instead, he took the confession of faith as a shield, which says, “His truth will surround you like weapons. You will not be afraid of an arrow flying by day.”

As the courageous elder reflected on these things, he advanced toward the army with great boldness, even though arrows were being shot. The arrows were flying on either side of him, but none of them touched the noble man. When the imperial agent saw him displaying such great boldness, he marveled that none of the arrows had touched him and that none of the brothers had been harmed at all. They immediately dismounted from their horses, fell at the feet of Apa Longinus, and bowed before him and the brothers with him, asking forgiveness for the reckless act they had committed. When Apa Longinus saw their repentance and their faith, he spoke to the imperial agent and the soldiers, saying: “Look, you have seen that we have struggled and have prepared ourselves to fight to the death for the faith of the fathers. We ask you to come to the monastery of the Enaton, where our fathers are, so that we may question them in the presence of your authority, to give you full assurance. Whatever they command us in your presence, we are ready to obey their word.”

The brothers were amazed at the words Father Longinus was speaking before the governor and his troops. They said to one another, “Did any of us remain in the monastery without coming here?” Then they approached their father, Father Longinus, saying, “Our father, do you not know that we are all here, and none of us is outside? How can we trouble these men and bother them to come to the monastery?” But he gave them no answer, since he knew what he was going to do. Then they all followed him—the imperial official and all the brothers. He walked ahead of them until he brought them to the tombs containing the other [?] fathers, the elders who had preceded him. These had firmly preserved the sound faith until the end of their lives, in accordance with what pleased God. Then he stood among the tombs, stretched out his hands, and prayed. He instructed them to pray with him. When he finished the prayer, they all said “Amen” together.

Father Longinus opened his mouth and raised his voice before them, saying, “My holy fathers, is it indeed God's will that we accept Leo's doctrine and sign it?” Immediately a voice came from the tombs containing the bodies of the saints, saying three times, “A curse upon the doctrine of the impious Leo! Do not utter his name with your mouths, nor share communion with anyone who accepts that doctrine. A curse upon those who sign Leo's Tome, the blasphemy of Leo! For it is full of blasphemy against the divinity of Christ, dividing it into two natures after the union of Christ.” When the imperial official and all the troops following them heard this voice coming from among the bodies of the saints, they were utterly astonished. They fell at the feet of Father Longinus and the other monks with him, asking them to forgive them and pray for them, so that they might come to the knowledge of the truth. Immediately many of the troops renounced their military service and the affairs of this empty life. They became monks and placed themselves under the authority of the holy Father Longinus because of the fear that had come upon them.

The imperial official and the remaining soldiers returned to the city, recounting the wonders they had seen. When the people of the city heard of the mighty deeds and wonders that had taken place through Father Longinus, they were strengthened still further in the faith. They went together to the governor's headquarters and brought out Acacius, the prefect, who was forcing them to accept communion with Leo's Tome. They burned him in the middle of the city. I say that they did not simply subject him to the disgrace of such a death; rather, it was a sentence of God's judgment, pronounced through the mouth of the great Father Longinus and the brothers with him, like the prophecy that our king David uttered in the tenth psalm, singing in this way: “Fire and sulfur are the portion of their cup.” When the bishop of that heresy saw the turmoil that had arisen, he changed his appearance, put on secular clothes, and left the city. He fled because of the fear that had come upon him, and he has not been found to this day. The church proclaimed openly the doctrines of the orthodox faith and advanced daily through the intercession of the Holy Spirit.

After this struggle, which the blessed Apa Longinus endured, he spent another twenty years governing the monasteries of the lavra. He was found worthy to lay his hands over the eyes of his father Apa Lucius, just as Joseph laid his hands over the eyes of his father Jacob. Apa Longinus cared for the brothers with every kind of understanding, and he instructed them to flee from empty glory, which is the beginning of all the passions. For through empty glory comes the love of money, which is the root of evils. The love of money produces anger; anger produces pride; anger produces envy, that evil beast. He also used to teach them to attend diligently to their manual work at the proper time and to hold their communal worship in the fear of God. He made himself an example to them in everything, caring tenderly for them all, both through bodily nourishment and through the teaching of the Lord. For he lived among them like a bishop, and everyone who wished to live according to the law of God looked to him and set their lives straight according to his virtues. For who hated empty glory as he did? Or who was as exalted in his deeds and as humble in his thoughts as this man? He was humble in every way, with his face lowered, conducting himself wisely. For he did not put on a false appearance like the people of our time, who outwardly adopt the appearance of godliness while their inner selves are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness. Who was as patient as this man, bearing patiently with those who had stumbled through their offenses until he restored them once again to their former state?

While he was living in this way, he departed to the Lord whom he loved on the second day of Meshir. He rested with all his fathers, whom he had resembled in his good deeds and his way of life: the patriarchs, the prophets, the apostles, and all the saints who had done the will of God. Oh, how great was the grief on the day when he went to his rest! Not only the monastic brothers but also the city of Alexandria and its districts, especially the people of the surrounding area, cried out loudly and with tears because such a father had been taken from them. Indeed, the sound of their weeping mingled with the hymn they were singing. The old people were looking for the staff of their old age; the young people, for the bridle of their self-control; those who had newly entered a life of obedience were looking for the one who would lead them into the kingdom of heaven; the married people, for their lawgiver; the poor, for the one who cared for them; and the sick, for the one who healed their illnesses, whether of the soul or of the body. In short, whether they were monks or laypeople, he cared for them all so that they might be saved, presenting them all as holy to the Lord Jesus Christ. Glory to him, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, who is of the same essence and gives life, now and always, forever and ever. Amen.
